Abstract:

The development of efficient and environmentally benign materials for energy conversion and optoelectronic applications remains a central challenge in modern materials chemistry. Hybrid lead halides have demonstrated remarkable optoelectronic performance, owing to their strong light absorption and intense luminescence properties. However, their practical deployment is hindered by poor environmental stability and inherent toxicity. Lead-free organic&ndashinorganic hybrid metal halides (OIMHs) incorporating metal centres such as Sb, Bi, Sn, and Mn etc have emerged as promising alternatives. These materials have attracted considerable attention owing to their structural tunability, cost-effective synthesis, and excellent optoelectronic properties, making them suitable for applications in photovoltaics, light-emitting diodes, scintillators, and photodetectors. Among them, zero-dimensional (0D) OIMHs, formed by the incorporation of bulky organic cations that isolate metal halide clusters, exhibit strong quantum confinement, soft deformable lattices, and enhanced electron&ndashphonon coupling. These features facilitate the formation of self-trapped excitons (STEs), leading to efficient broadband emission and making them highly promising candidates for next-generation energy conversion and optoelectronic technologies. Moreover, understanding of the relationship between the structural distortion and luminescence properties of these materials is of utmost importance for tuning the emission properties for various practical applications. We have synthesized several novel Bi/Sb-based metal halides and systematically investigated their structural and photophysical properties using both experimental and theoretical techniques.
